note: Hover and tap explainers for the Off the Prior site.

entries.title: Timestral
entries.body: Mistral's family of open forecasting models, released October 15, 2026, in four sizes: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters (the M is millions). Give it the history of a number and it returns 21 guesses per future step, from very low to very high.

entries.title: Forecast
entries.body: A guess about future values of a series, made only from its past (and sometimes from helper series). A good forecast is not always right; it is right about how unsure it should be.

entries.title: Quantiles
entries.body: Instead of one guess, Timestral gives 21: the value it thinks has a 1% chance of being undershot, 5%, 10%, and so on up to 99%. The 10% and 90% ones bound an '80% band' that the truth should land in about 8 times out of 10.

entries.title: Prior
entries.body: Everything a model assumes before it sees your data. Timestral learned its prior mostly from made-up series (trend + season + noise), so 'off the prior' means series that don't look like that.

entries.title: Synthetic data
entries.body: Series generated by a program instead of measured in the world. Cheap, endless, and only as varied as the program that makes them.

entries.title: History (context)
entries.body: The stretch of past values the model reads before forecasting. Timestral can read up to 32,768 steps.

entries.title: Horizon
entries.body: How many steps ahead the forecast goes. Here: 16, 128 or 1,024.

entries.title: Patch
entries.body: Timestral chops the history into pieces of 32 steps and treats each piece the way a language model treats a word.

entries.title: Referee (oracle)
entries.body: A forecaster that cheats legally: it knows the exact equations and the exact hidden state of the simulator at the moment the history ends, and runs the simulator forward 500 times. Nobody can do better on average, so it marks the best achievable forecast.

entries.title: MASE
entries.body: Mean absolute scaled error: the average miss of the middle guess, divided by how badly 'tomorrow equals today' (or 'same as last season') does on the history. Below 1 beats that naive rule.

entries.title: CRPS
entries.body: A score for the whole spread of guesses, not just the middle one. It punishes being wrong and being overconfident. Lower is better.

entries.title: Error ratio
entries.body: Timestral's error divided by the referee's error on the same series. 1 means as good as the referee; 3 means three times worse. Averages here are geometric means, so a 2x and a 0.5x cancel out.

entries.title: Geometric mean
entries.body: Multiply n numbers and take the n-th root. The right average for ratios: 2x worse and 2x better average to 1, not 1.25.

entries.title: Old-school methods
entries.body: Three forecasters from before deep learning: 'repeat the last season' (seasonal naive), exponential smoothing (ETS) and ARIMA. Fast, explainable, and the usual yardstick.

entries.title: Chaos
entries.body: Fully deterministic rules whose tiny differences grow exponentially, so long-range prediction is impossible even with perfect equations. Short-range prediction is very possible, which is where the gap lives.

entries.title: Lyapunov time
entries.body: How long a chaotic system takes to blow a tiny error up by a factor of e (about 2.7). After ten of them, nobody can forecast it, referee included.

entries.title: Mackey-Glass
entries.body: A delay equation first written for blood-cell production: today's change depends on the value some time τ ago. Gives smooth, almost-repeating wiggles.

entries.title: Kuramoto oscillators
entries.body: Many little clocks that nudge each other. Weak coupling: they drift independently. Strong coupling: they sync. In between is the hardest.

entries.title: Regime switch
entries.body: The rules of a series change at some moment: the level jumps, the season changes its length, or the noise grows or shrinks.

entries.title: Heavy tails
entries.body: Distributions where huge jumps are rare but not rare enough to ignore. Think market crashes, floods and earthquakes.

entries.title: Linear readout
entries.body: A test of what a model knows inside: fit a straight-line formula from its internal numbers to some quantity. If the formula works, the information is in there, used or not.

entries.title: Attention
entries.body: The part of a transformer that lets each piece of the input look at the others and decide which ones matter.

entries.title: Helper series (covariate)
entries.body: A second series fed to the model to help forecast the main one, like temperature for electricity demand. 'Known-future' means its future is given too.

entries.title: Method of analogues
entries.body: A very old trick: find the moments in the history that look most like now and see what happened next. No training at all.

entries.title: Benchmark
entries.body: A fixed set of test series plus a scoring rule, so different models can be compared fairly.

entries.title: Fine-tuning
entries.body: Training an already-trained model a little more on new examples. Full fine-tuning updates every weight; LoRA updates small add-on matrices instead.

entries.title: Failure search
entries.body: Letting an optimizer (CMA-ES, MAP-Elites or plain gradients) tweak a series generator to make Timestral miss as badly as possible.

entries.title: Neuron (and its two poles)
entries.body: One unit of a layer's MLP. In Timestral's SwiGLU layers a neuron's value can be positive or negative, so each neuron is studied as two halves, called poles.

entries.title: Parameters
entries.body: The numbers a model learns. Timestral-209M has about 209 million.
